description: Common True Katydids are secondary consumers. Although they mostly eat plants including deciduous foliage, they are also known to sometimes consume small insects like aphids. They are very well camouflaged by their wings which resemble extremely realistic leaves. They are closely related to crickets and grasshoppers, but they have much longer antennae and their wings are held over their body vertically like the roof of a house.  In contrast with other katydids, they do not fly often and instead walk and hop. The Common True Katydid makes a very distinct noise that sounds like "Katy did, Katy didn't" repeated at night, as they are mostly nocturnal. The female has an ovipositor protruding from the back of the abdomen. Females lay eggs in rows on plant stems. Nymphs hatch from the eggs and molt several times before becoming adults. They live for about a year. They are found in the eastern half of America as far north as the Adirondacks and as far south as northern Florida. They are often found high in trees. One potential predator is the Little Brown Bat, one potential competitor is the Bush Katydid, and one potential prey is the Sugar Maple Tree.
